items.e: The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 3 of Shemonah Perakim, and these are his words: “The ancients said that the soul has health and illness just as the body has health and illness. The health of the soul is that its disposition should be such… that it continually performs good and proper deeds. And its illness is that its disposition should be such… that it continually performs bad and disgraceful deeds. And just as those with bodily illnesses, when they become aware of their sickness, ask the physicians who inform them of what they must do and warn them accordingly…, so too, those whose souls are ill must seek out the sages, who are the physicians of the soul…, and they will heal them through the practices by which the dispositions of the soul are healed…”— so far are his words; see there. And likewise the Rambam wrote in Chapter 2 of Hilchot De’ot, relating the illness of the soul to the illness of the body; see there.

And behold, just as in the processes of the body’s wellbeing—its vitality, its health, and its structure—it is already known that over the course of generations, human strength continually declines, until in our generation, due to our many sins, health has diminished and weakness has increased. Illness and pain, of every affliction and every disease, affect a great number of people. So too is it with the processes of the soul’s wellbeing: the life of the spirit does not remain firm in its place. Generation after generation, the spiritual condition has declined; the health of the soul diminishes, and those stricken and afflicted with the sickness of the soul grow ever more numerous with time.

Indeed, in earlier generations, it was only over the course of an entire generation—from fathers to grandchildren—that a shift could be felt in the state of Torah and reverence when compared with the preceding generation. But now, in this last generation, alas, due to our many sins, within the span of but a few short years, a new spirit passes over the face of the people. It carries upon its wings a multitude of changes, an endless host of transformations. Already one can see and sense a great alteration: a deepening weakness and enfeeblement of the soul in matters of Torah, reverence, and the service of the Blessed One. These go on steadily diminishing, until this dark hour in which the sicknesses of the soul have encompassed almost all flesh—may God have mercy.

And when we look with discerning eyes upon the state of Torah and reverence in general, to see in which of them the sickness of the soul has prevailed more grievously, it is plain to the eye that there is no comparison between the weakness of Torah and the frailty of reverence. For behold, despite all the tribulations that have befallen our holy Torah—its diminished esteem and the desolation of its gates—nevertheless, the promise of the Giver of the Torah, blessed be His Name, remains steadfast: that the testimony shall not be forgotten from the mouth of the seed of Jacob. This has sustained us even to this very day. For the voice, the voice of Jacob (Gen. 27:22), is still heard in the houses of study, and the gates of Zion, distinguished by the learning of halachah, are wide open. And thus there are found, blessed be the Lord, pure-hearted ones who support it with in their decisions and their responses.
